case: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period. She has always been the shortest student in her class. Height is 142 cm (below the 1st percentile). Pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg in both arms. Physical examination shows a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a low posterior hairline, and webbing of the neck. Breasts are Tanner stage 1, and pubic hair is sparse. Serum studies show an FSH concentration of 92 mIU/mL (normal 3 to 10), LH concentration of 38 mIU/mL (normal 2 to 12), and estradiol concentration of less than 10 pg/mL (normal 30 to 100). Pelvic ultrasonography shows a small prepubertal uterus and bilateral streak gonads. Karyotype of peripheral blood lymphocytes is 45,X in all cells counted. Diagnosis: Turner syndrome with primary amenorrhea.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's serum FSH concentration?
options: Autonomous secretion by a pituitary gonadotroph adenoma
Loss of negative feedback by ovarian estradiol and inhibin
Reduced hepatic clearance of circulating gonadotropins
Ectopic FSH production by a dysgerminoma in a streak gonad
approach: Note the pattern: high FSH and LH with very low estradiol. This is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, which points to failure of the gonad itself.
Link 45,X to ovarian dysgenesis: oocytes are lost early, so the gonads become fibrous streaks with no follicles.
Without follicles there is no estradiol or inhibin to hold FSH down, so FSH rises.
questions.why: In Turner syndrome the fetal ovary starts with germ cells, but they undergo accelerated atresia, and by puberty the ovaries are fibrous streaks without follicles. Granulosa cells of growing follicles make estradiol and inhibin, and both normally suppress FSH secretion. With no follicles, that feedback is gone, so the pituitary releases large amounts of FSH and LH. The low estradiol explains the absent breast development and the prepubertal uterus.
whyNot: A gonadotroph adenoma is rare, would not cause the streak gonads, and usually presents with mass effects. The low estradiol here shows the problem is a lack of feedback, not a pituitary tumor.
Correct.
Liver disease does not raise gonadotropins to this degree. The pattern of high FSH with absent estradiol reflects gonadal failure.
Dysgerminoma risk rises in streak gonads that contain Y chromosome material, which this 45,X patient lacks. Germ cell tumors can make hCG, AFP, or LDH, not FSH.

questions.stem: Prenatal ultrasonography during her mother's pregnancy showed a large fluid-filled mass at the back of the fetal neck. Which of the following best explains how that finding relates to this patient's neck appearance now?
options: Persistence of a second pharyngeal cleft remnant
Fibrosis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle in utero
Persistence of a remnant of the thyroglossal duct
Regression of a jugular lymphatic cystic hygroma
approach: Identify the prenatal mass: a posterior neck fluid collection in a 45,X fetus is a cystic hygroma.
Recall that the lymphatic system develops abnormally in Turner syndrome, so lymph collects in the neck and limbs.
When the hygroma later drains and shrinks, the stretched skin remains as webbing.
questions.why: Fetuses with Turner syndrome often have delayed or abnormal connection of the jugular lymph sacs to the venous system. Lymph pools at the back of the neck as a cystic hygroma. If the fetus survives, the fluid is resorbed, and the stretched skin folds remain as a webbed neck with a low posterior hairline. The same lymphatic problem causes the puffy hands and feet (lymphedema) seen in newborn girls with Turner syndrome. Short stature in Turner syndrome is a separate effect, from loss of one copy of the SHOX gene.
whyNot: A second pharyngeal cleft remnant forms a cyst or sinus along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not posterior neck webbing.
Fibrosis of the sternocleidomastoid causes congenital torticollis, with the head tilted to one side, not bilateral webbing.
A thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline anterior neck mass that moves upward when the tongue protrudes.
Correct.

questions.stem: A buccal mucosal smear is prepared from this patient and from her 46,XX sister, and the nuclei are examined for sex chromatin. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: No Barr body in the patient and one Barr body in her sister
One Barr body in the patient and one Barr body in her sister
No Barr body in the patient and two Barr bodies in her sister
One Barr body in the patient and two Barr bodies in her sister
approach: Recall the rule: every X chromosome beyond the first is inactivated, so the number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one.
Apply it to each karyotype: 45,X has one X, so zero Barr bodies. 46,XX has two X chromosomes, so one Barr body.
questions.why: Early in female development, XIST RNA coats one X chromosome in each cell and silences most of its genes. The silenced X condenses into heterochromatin that is seen at the edge of the nucleus as a Barr body. A cell keeps only one active X, so the number of Barr bodies is the number of X chromosomes minus one. A 45,X cell has a single active X and no Barr body, and a 46,XX cell has one.
whyNot: Correct.
A single X is never inactivated, because each cell needs one active X. A 45,X cell has no Barr body.
A 46,XX cell inactivates only one of its two X chromosomes, so it has one Barr body. Two Barr bodies are seen in 47,XXX cells.
Both counts are one too high. One Barr body would be expected in a 46,XX or 47,XXY cell, and two in a 47,XXX cell.

questions.stem: Laparoscopic biopsy of the left gonad shows wavy fibrous stroma resembling ovarian stroma. Which of the following structures, the most numerous follicle type in the ovary of a healthy girl her age, is most likely absent from this tissue?
options: A fluid-filled antrum with the oocyte on a cumulus oophorus
A primary oocyte with a zona pellucida and stratified granulosa
A primary oocyte within one layer of flat follicular cells
A collapsed structure of large lipid-rich luteinized granulosa cells
approach: Recall that most follicles in the ovary at any age after birth are resting primordial follicles.
Match the description: a primordial follicle is a primary oocyte surrounded by one layer of flattened follicular (pregranulosa) cells.
Recognize that a streak gonad has lost its follicles, so even primordial follicles are missing.
questions.why: At puberty each ovary still holds a large reserve of primordial follicles, far more than any other follicle type. A primordial follicle is a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I with a single layer of flat follicular cells around it. As a follicle grows, the cells become cuboidal (primary follicle), then stratified with a zona pellucida, then form an antrum (secondary follicle), and finally a large mature (Graafian) follicle. In Turner syndrome the oocytes undergo accelerated atresia during fetal life and early childhood, so the streak contains only stroma.
whyNot: An antrum with the oocyte sitting on a cumulus oophorus describes a mature (Graafian) follicle. Only one or a few are present in a cycle, so they are never the most numerous type.
A zona pellucida with several layers of granulosa cells describes a growing preantral follicle. These are recruited in small numbers from the primordial pool.
Correct.
Large lipid-rich luteinized cells describe the corpus luteum, which forms after ovulation and is not a follicle.

dx: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) with infertility and gynecomastia
case: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because they have been unable to conceive after 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse. He shaves only once a week. Height is 191 cm, with long legs relative to his trunk. Pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows bilateral, symmetric breast enlargement and sparse body hair. Both testes are small and firm, each with a volume of 3 mL (normal 15 to 25). Semen analysis shows no sperm. Serum studies show an FSH concentration of 41 mIU/mL (normal 1.5 to 12.4), LH concentration of 24 mIU/mL (normal 1.7 to 8.6), and total testosterone concentration of 190 ng/dL (normal 300 to 1000). Karyotype is 47,XXY in all 30 cells counted. Diagnosis: Klinefelter syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional laboratory findings most directly reflects damage to this patient's seminiferous tubules?
approach: Separate the two compartments of the testis: seminiferous tubules (Sertoli and germ cells) and the interstitium (Leydig cells).
Recall that Sertoli cells make inhibin B, which suppresses FSH, while Leydig cells make testosterone, which mainly suppresses LH.
Pick the marker that comes from the tubules: inhibin B.
questions.why: Klinefelter syndrome causes progressive hyalinization and fibrosis of the seminiferous tubules. Sertoli cells in the tubules make inhibin B, so its level falls, and FSH rises because inhibin B normally suppresses FSH. Leydig cell dysfunction is a separate problem that lowers testosterone and raises LH. That is why both gonadotropins are high in this patient, and why inhibin B is the marker that tracks tubule damage.
whyNot: Low testosterone reflects Leydig cell dysfunction in the interstitium, not tubule damage.
High LH is the pituitary response to low testosterone, so it reflects Leydig cell failure.
Correct.
Estradiol rises because LH drives aromatase activity in the testis and because body fat converts androgens to estrogen. It does not measure tubule function.

questions.stem: DNA marker studies show that both of his X chromosomes are maternal in origin and are heterozygous for markers close to the centromere. Which of the following events most likely produced his karyotype?
approach: Both X chromosomes are maternal, so the error happened in the egg, not the sperm.
Markers near the centromere stay with their own homolog until meiosis I separates the homologs. Different (heterozygous) centromere markers mean both homologs went into the egg.
That pattern fits failure of homologs to separate in meiosis I. A uniform 47,XXY karyotype in all cells argues against a later mitotic error.
questions.why: In meiosis I, the two homologous chromosomes separate. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids separate. Because crossing over rarely reaches the centromere, the region near the centromere keeps the identity of its original homolog. If an egg receives two X chromosomes that differ at the centromere, both homologs were kept together, which is nondisjunction in meiosis I. A meiosis II error would give two copies of the same homolog at the centromere. Nondisjunction after fertilization usually produces mosaicism, such as 46,XY/47,XXY, with a milder phenotype.
whyNot: Correct.
A meiosis II error separates sister chromatids incorrectly, so both X chromosomes would be identical (homozygous) at centromeric markers.
A paternal meiosis I error produces an XY sperm, so one of the two X chromosomes would be paternal. Here both are maternal.
A mitotic error after fertilization usually produces mosaicism. All 30 cells here were 47,XXY, so the error came before fertilization.

topics: Meiosis I versus meiosis II nondisjunction

questions.stem: Examination of the breasts shows a soft, rubbery, mobile disc of tissue centered under each areola. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Clonal proliferation of ductal epithelium after BRCA2 loss
Prolactin excess stimulating lobular milk production
Adipose tissue deposition without glandular tissue
Higher ratio of estrogen to androgen effect on the breast
approach: Recognize gynecomastia: bilateral, symmetric, soft, mobile subareolar tissue in a man.
Link it to the hormone balance: estrogen stimulates ductal and stromal growth, and androgen opposes it.
In Klinefelter syndrome testosterone is low, and high LH drives testicular aromatase, so the estrogen to androgen ratio rises.
questions.why: Gynecomastia is benign growth of breast ducts and surrounding stroma in a male. It occurs whenever estrogen effect outweighs androgen effect. In Klinefelter syndrome, testosterone is low and high LH increases aromatization of testosterone to estradiol in the testis, so the ratio shifts toward estrogen. Men with Klinefelter syndrome also have a much higher risk of male breast carcinoma than other men. A hard, eccentric, fixed mass would raise that concern and needs biopsy.
whyNot: Clonal ductal proliferation describes carcinoma. Male breast carcinoma is linked to BRCA2 and Klinefelter syndrome, but it presents as a hard, usually one-sided mass, often eccentric and fixed.
Prolactin causes galactorrhea and suppresses GnRH, but it does not explain soft bilateral glandular discs in this setting.
Fat without glandular tissue is pseudogynecomastia, seen in obesity. It feels soft and diffuse, with no firm disc under the areola.
Correct.

questions.stem: A testicular biopsy shows hyalinized seminiferous tubules with no germ cells. Between the tubules are clusters of large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. These interstitial cells are the normal source of which of the following?
approach: Locate the cells: they lie in the interstitium between tubules, not inside the tubules.
Large polygonal eosinophilic interstitial cells are Leydig cells.
Leydig cells make testosterone under LH stimulation. The other options are Sertoli cell products.
questions.why: Leydig cells sit in the connective tissue between seminiferous tubules. They are large and polygonal, with eosinophilic, lipid-rich cytoplasm, and they make testosterone in response to LH. In Klinefelter syndrome, the tubules scar down and Leydig cells appear clustered (pseudohyperplasia), yet they produce too little testosterone. Sertoli cells sit inside the tubules on the basement membrane and make inhibin B, androgen-binding protein, and, in the fetus, anti-Mullerian hormone.
whyNot: Inhibin B is made by Sertoli cells inside the tubules and feeds back to suppress FSH.
Correct.
Androgen-binding protein is made by Sertoli cells and keeps testosterone concentrated in the tubule lumen.
Anti-Mullerian hormone is made by fetal Sertoli cells and causes the paramesonephric ducts to regress.

dx: Fragile X syndrome in a teenage boy whose mother has primary ovarian insufficiency from an FMR1 premutation
case: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician for evaluation of learning problems. He has moderate intellectual disability, avoids eye contact, and has hand-flapping behavior. Pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a long narrow face, a prominent jaw, large protruding ears, and hyperextensible finger joints. Pubertal development is Tanner stage 5, and each testis has a volume of 40 mL (normal 15 to 25). His 38-year-old mother has had no menstrual periods for 2 years, with hot flashes. Molecular testing shows more than 200 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene of the boy (normal fewer than 45) and 85 repeats in his mother. Diagnosis: fragile X syndrome in the son and FMR1 premutation with primary ovarian insufficiency in the mother.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the absence of FMR1 protein in this patient's cells?
options: Toxic gain of function from an expanded CAG polyglutamine tract
Premature stop codon from a nonsense point mutation in the gene
Abnormal mRNA processing from an intronic GAA repeat expansion
Methylation of the expanded repeat silencing transcription
approach: Identify the mutation: more than 200 CGG repeats in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 is a full mutation.
Recall what a full mutation does: the repeat and nearby promoter become hypermethylated, and transcription stops.
No mRNA means no FMR1 protein, which is needed for normal synapse function.
questions.why: Fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of a CGG repeat in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 on the X chromosome. Above about 200 repeats, the repeat and the promoter become heavily methylated, the chromatin closes, and the gene is silenced. The repeat tends to expand further when passed through the mother, so each generation can be more severely affected (anticipation). The missing protein normally regulates translation at synapses, which explains the intellectual disability. The large testes appear after puberty.
whyNot: An expanded CAG tract that adds polyglutamine to a protein causes Huntington disease and some spinocerebellar ataxias. These are toxic gain-of-function disorders.
A nonsense mutation can cause loss of function in many genes, but this patient's testing shows a repeat expansion, not a point mutation.
An intronic GAA expansion in the frataxin gene causes Friedreich ataxia by reducing transcription, not fragile X syndrome.
Correct.

questions.stem: The oocyte that gave rise to this patient was already present in his mother's ovary when she was born. At that time, the oocyte was arrested at which of the following stages?
approach: Recall that all oogonia enter meiosis before birth, becoming primary oocytes.
Primary oocytes stop in prophase I (diplotene) and stay there until a surge of LH just before ovulation, which may be decades later.
Meiosis I finishes at ovulation, and the oocyte then arrests in metaphase II until fertilization.
questions.why: Oogenesis starts before birth. Oogonia multiply in the fetal ovary, replicate their DNA, and enter meiosis I as primary oocytes, then stop in prophase I. Each one waits in a primordial follicle until it is selected for ovulation. Just before ovulation it completes meiosis I and releases the first polar body, then arrests again in metaphase II. Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters. Spermatogenesis differs: it starts at puberty, runs continuously, and each meiosis yields four sperm instead of one egg.
whyNot: Oogonia are in mitotic interphase, but by birth they have all entered meiosis. None remain as dividing oogonia.
Correct.
Metaphase I is passed quickly during the hours before ovulation. It is not an arrest point.
Metaphase II is the second arrest point, reached at ovulation and held until fertilization. It occurs decades after birth.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely in this patient's mother?
options: Low FSH and low estradiol concentrations
Low FSH and high estradiol concentrations
High FSH and low estradiol concentrations
High FSH and high estradiol concentrations
approach: Recognize primary ovarian insufficiency: loss of ovarian function with amenorrhea and hot flashes before age 40.
Link it to the FMR1 premutation (about 55 to 200 repeats), a known cause of early follicle loss.
Failure of the ovary itself means low estradiol, and loss of feedback means high FSH.
questions.why: Primary ovarian insufficiency is loss of ovarian function before age 40. Causes include Turner syndrome, the FMR1 premutation, autoimmune oophoritis, and chemotherapy or radiation. Women with a premutation do not have fragile X syndrome, but about one in five develop ovarian insufficiency. With few follicles left, estradiol and inhibin fall, the pituitary loses negative feedback, and FSH rises, usually into the menopausal range. Low estradiol causes the hot flashes and amenorrhea.
whyNot: Low FSH with low estradiol is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, from a hypothalamic or pituitary cause such as low body weight or a pituitary mass.
Low FSH with high estradiol suggests an estrogen-secreting source, such as a granulosa cell tumor, suppressing the pituitary.
Correct.
High FSH with high estradiol would mean the pituitary is overdriving a working ovary. That does not fit an ovary that has stopped producing follicles.

questions.stem: During measurement of testicular volume, the physician strokes the skin of the boy's upper medial thigh, and the testis on that side rises. The muscle layer of the spermatic cord responsible for this movement is continuous with which of the following structures?
approach: Identify the reflex: stroking the medial thigh raises the testis, which is the cremasteric reflex.
The cremaster muscle and fascia form the middle covering of the spermatic cord.
Recall that each cord layer comes from an abdominal wall layer: the cremaster comes from the internal oblique.
questions.why: As the testis descends through the inguinal canal, it carries a covering from each layer of the abdominal wall. The external spermatic fascia comes from the external oblique aponeurosis, the cremaster muscle and fascia come from the internal oblique, and the internal spermatic fascia comes from the transversalis fascia. The tunica vaginalis is a pouch of peritoneum around the testis. The cremaster contracts in the cremasteric reflex, and the motor limb of that reflex is the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
whyNot: Correct.
The external oblique aponeurosis forms the external spermatic fascia, a thin outer layer with no muscle.
The transversalis fascia forms the internal spermatic fascia, the innermost covering of the cord.
The parietal peritoneum forms the tunica vaginalis around the testis, not a muscle layer of the cord.

case: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period. Breast development began at age 11. Height is 172 cm. Pulse is 68/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows Tanner stage 4 breasts and scant pubic and axillary hair. External genitalia appear female, and the vagina ends in a blind pouch 4 cm deep. A firm, mobile mass is palpated in each inguinal canal. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no uterus. Serum testosterone concentration is 640 ng/dL (normal adult female 15 to 70, adult male 300 to 1000), LH concentration is 19 mIU/mL (normal adult male 1.7 to 8.6), and estradiol concentration is 58 pg/mL (normal adult male 10 to 40). Karyotype is 46,XY. Diagnosis: complete androgen insensitivity syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's breast development?
options: Aromatization of testosterone with no opposing androgen effect
Estradiol secretion by residual ovarian tissue in a streak gonad
Prolactin excess from a lactotroph adenoma of the pituitary gland
Adrenal estrogen secretion driven by increased ACTH stimulation
approach: Identify the defect: a nonfunctional androgen receptor, so tissues cannot respond to testosterone or DHT.
The hypothalamus and pituitary also ignore testosterone, so LH and testosterone rise.
Aromatase in the testes and fat converts the extra testosterone to estradiol, which acts on the breast without androgen to oppose it.
questions.why: Complete androgen insensitivity is an X-linked defect of the androgen receptor. Because androgen feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary does not work, LH rises and drives the testes to make more testosterone. Aromatase turns some of it into estradiol. Estrogen receptors work normally, and no androgen action opposes them, so breasts develop well at puberty. Pubic and axillary hair depend on androgen action, so they stay scant.
whyNot: Correct.
This patient has testes, not ovaries or streak gonads. The inguinal masses are the testes.
Prolactin causes milk secretion and suppresses gonadotropins. It would not raise LH and testosterone.
Adrenal estrogen excess with high ACTH is not part of this condition. Cortisol synthesis is normal.

questions.stem: A 46,XY newborn with 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency also has female-appearing external genitalia. Which of the following internal structures is most likely present in that newborn but absent in this patient?
approach: Sort male internal structures by the hormone they need: Wolffian derivatives need testosterone, while external genitalia and prostate need DHT.
In 5-alpha-reductase deficiency testosterone acts normally, so Wolffian structures form. In androgen insensitivity neither hormone can act.
Both conditions have testes making anti-Mullerian hormone, so Mullerian structures are absent in both.
questions.why: Testosterone acts directly on the androgen receptor to keep the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts and turn them into the epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicles. DHT, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, is needed to form the penis, scrotum, and prostate. In 5-alpha-reductase deficiency the Wolffian structures form normally, but the external genitalia are undervirilized. In complete androgen insensitivity, the receptor fails, so neither Wolffian structures nor male external genitalia develop.
whyNot: The uterine tubes come from the paramesonephric ducts. Anti-Mullerian hormone from the testes causes them to regress in both conditions.
The upper third of the vagina is a paramesonephric derivative, so it is absent in both conditions.
The uterus is a paramesonephric derivative and regresses under anti-Mullerian hormone in both conditions.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the absence of a uterus in this patient?
options: Anti-Mullerian hormone from fetal Sertoli cells
Dihydrotestosterone formed in the urogenital sinus
Failure of the paramesonephric ducts to form
approach: The uterus comes from the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts.
A 46,XY fetus with testes makes anti-Mullerian hormone from Sertoli cells, which causes those ducts to regress.
The androgen receptor defect does not affect anti-Mullerian hormone signaling, so the ducts regress normally.
questions.why: SRY drives the gonad to become a testis with Sertoli cells. Fetal Sertoli cells secrete anti-Mullerian hormone, which acts through its own receptor to make the paramesonephric ducts regress. This pathway does not need the androgen receptor, so it works normally in androgen insensitivity. As a result, the uterus, tubes, and upper vagina are absent, and the vagina is a short blind pouch formed from the urogenital sinus.
whyNot: Testosterone keeps the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts. It does not cause Mullerian regression, and it cannot act in this patient.
Correct.
DHT shapes the external genitalia and prostate. It has no role in Mullerian regression, and it cannot act here.
The paramesonephric ducts form in every embryo. Failure of the ducts to develop is the defect in Mullerian agenesis, which occurs in 46,XX individuals with ovaries.

questions.stem: The patient's 19-year-old cousin has had regular menstrual periods since age 12 but has had no menses for the past 4 months. She is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the cousin's amenorrhea?
approach: Classify the amenorrhea: menses were regular and have now stopped for more than 3 months, so it is secondary.
Recall that pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea.
Contrast with the patient in the case, who has primary amenorrhea because she has never menstruated by age 15 despite breast development.
questions.why: Primary amenorrhea means no menarche by age 15, or by age 13 with no breast development. Secondary amenorrhea means no menses for 3 months in someone who had regular cycles. The cousin has secondary amenorrhea, and pregnancy is the most common cause, so it is checked first with an hCG test. The case patient has primary amenorrhea from an absent uterus.
whyNot: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea follows low energy intake, heavy exercise, or stress. Nothing in this history suggests it, and pregnancy is far more common.
Hyperprolactinemia can cause secondary amenorrhea, often with galactorrhea, but it is much less common than pregnancy.
Correct.
Polycystic ovary syndrome usually causes irregular cycles from menarche onward, often with hirsutism, rather than sudden loss of regular cycles.

dx: Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome), with imperforate hymen as the key differential
case: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period. She has no cyclic abdominal or pelvic pain. Breast development began at age 10. Height is 163 cm. Pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows Tanner stage 5 breasts and Tanner stage 5 pubic and axillary hair. External genitalia are normal, and the vagina is a blind pouch 2 cm deep with no bulging membrane. Pelvic ultrasonography shows normal ovaries and no uterus. Serum FSH concentration is 6 mIU/mL (normal 3 to 10), and testosterone concentration is 38 ng/dL (normal 15 to 70). Karyotype is 46,XX. Diagnosis: Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome).

questions.stem: Before the karyotype result was available, which of the following findings most strongly favored this diagnosis over complete androgen insensitivity?
options: Tanner stage 5 pubic and axillary hair
Vagina ending in a short blind pouch
approach: List what the two conditions share: primary amenorrhea, breast development, a blind vaginal pouch, and no uterus.
Find the difference: pubic and axillary hair need androgen action, which is absent in complete androgen insensitivity.
Normal hair growth means working androgen receptors, which fits a 46,XX patient with normal ovaries.
questions.why: Both Mullerian agenesis and complete androgen insensitivity cause primary amenorrhea with breasts, a short blind vagina, and no uterus. In Mullerian agenesis the patient is 46,XX with normal ovaries and normal androgen action, so pubic and axillary hair are normal and testosterone is in the female range. In complete androgen insensitivity the patient is 46,XY with testes and no functioning androgen receptor, so body hair is scant and testosterone is in the male range.
whyNot: Breasts develop in both conditions: from ovarian estrogen in Mullerian agenesis and from aromatized testosterone in androgen insensitivity.
Correct.
A short blind vaginal pouch occurs in both, because the upper vagina is missing in each.
The uterus is absent in both: never formed in Mullerian agenesis, and regressed under anti-Mullerian hormone in androgen insensitivity.

topics: Primary amenorrhea with a blind vaginal pouch

questions.stem: The short vaginal pouch present in this patient most likely developed from which of the following embryonic structures?
approach: Recall that the paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina.
In this patient those ducts failed to develop, yet a short vagina is present, so it must have another source.
The lower vagina comes from the sinovaginal bulbs of the urogenital sinus.
questions.why: The vagina has two origins. The paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts fuse in the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, while the uterine tubes come from their unfused upper parts. The lower vagina forms from the sinovaginal bulbs of the urogenital sinus, which grow up to meet the fused ducts. In Mullerian agenesis only the sinus-derived lower part forms, so the vagina is a short blind pouch. The ovaries come from the gonadal ridge, which is why they are normal.
whyNot: Correct.
The paramesonephric ducts form the upper vagina, uterus, and tubes. These are the structures that failed to develop here.
The mesonephric ducts form the epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicles in males and regress in females.
The genital tubercle forms the clitoris in females and the glans penis in males.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of findings in a 14-year-old girl with no menses would instead indicate an imperforate hymen?
options: Absent breast development, short stature, and a webbed neck
Normal breasts, absent pubic hair, and bilateral inguinal masses
Clitoral enlargement, deepening voice, and increased muscle mass
Monthly pelvic pain and a bluish bulging introital membrane
approach: An imperforate hymen leaves the uterus and ovaries normal, so menses begin but cannot flow out.
Blood collects in the vagina (hematocolpos), stretching the hymen and causing pain each month.
Pick the option with cyclic pain and a bulging blue-tinged membrane.
questions.why: The hymen is a thin membrane at the junction of the vaginal plate and the urogenital sinus that normally opens late in fetal life or around birth. If it stays closed, puberty proceeds normally and menstruation starts, but blood is trapped behind the membrane. The girl has primary amenorrhea with cyclic pelvic pain, and the membrane bulges and looks bluish from the blood behind it. A large hematocolpos can press on the bladder or rectum. Mullerian agenesis, by contrast, causes no cyclic pain because there is no endometrium.
whyNot: Absent breasts, short stature, and a webbed neck describe Turner syndrome with streak gonads.
Normal breasts with absent pubic hair and inguinal testes describe complete androgen insensitivity.
Clitoral enlargement, a deep voice, and more muscle mass are signs of virilization from androgen excess, not an outflow obstruction.
Correct.

topics: Outflow tract causes of primary amenorrhea

questions.stem: This patient's normal breast and pubic hair development shows that her hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis activated normally. The onset of gonadal puberty in this patient was most likely marked by which of the following?
options: A midcycle surge of LH from estradiol feedback
Pulses of LH secretion occurring during sleep
A rise in pituitary secretion of prolactin
approach: Recall that puberty begins when the hypothalamus restarts pulsatile GnRH release after the quiet years of childhood.
The first sign of this in the blood is LH pulses that appear at night during sleep.
Over time the pulses spread to the daytime, estradiol rises, and breast development begins.
questions.why: GnRH secretion is active in infancy, then suppressed through childhood. At puberty, the GnRH pulse generator reawakens, and the earliest sign is sleep-associated pulses of LH. Rising FSH and LH stimulate the ovaries to make estradiol. In girls the usual order is breast budding (thelarche), then pubic hair (pubarche), then the growth spurt, then menarche. This patient followed that sequence except menarche, which cannot occur without a uterus.
whyNot: Continuous GnRH desensitizes the gonadotroph receptors and suppresses LH and FSH. Puberty needs pulsatile GnRH.
The midcycle LH surge triggers ovulation in established cycles. It needs a mature follicle making high estradiol and comes late in puberty.
Correct.
Prolactin rises in pregnancy and with pituitary tumors. High prolactin suppresses GnRH and delays puberty.

dx: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency with virilized genitalia in a 46,XX newborn
case: A 10-day-old infant is brought to the emergency department because of poor feeding and vomiting for 2 days. At birth, the external genitalia were noted to be ambiguous. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 182/min, respirations are 48/min, and blood pressure is 58/32 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes, an enlarged clitoris, and partially fused, rugated labioscrotal folds. No gonads are palpable. Serum sodium concentration is 126 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), and potassium concentration is 7.0 mEq/L (normal 3.7 to 5.9). Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone concentration is more than 50 times the upper limit of normal for age. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a uterus and two ovaries. Karyotype is 46,XX. Diagnosis: classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions causes the same category of disorder of sex development as this infant's condition?
approach: Classify this infant: 46,XX with ovaries and virilized external genitalia is a 46,XX disorder of sex development (formerly female pseudohermaphroditism).
The cause is androgen exposure of a female fetus, from the fetal adrenal here.
Pick the other source of androgen exposure: an androgen-secreting tumor in the mother.
questions.why: In a 46,XX disorder of sex development, the gonads are ovaries and the internal organs are female, but the external genitalia are virilized by androgen during fetal life. The two classic sources are the fetal adrenal in congenital adrenal hyperplasia and the mother, for example an androgen-secreting luteoma of pregnancy or androgen medication. In a 46,XY disorder of sex development (formerly male pseudohermaphroditism), the gonads are testes, but the external genitalia are undervirilized, as in androgen insensitivity or 5-alpha-reductase deficiency.
whyNot: Complete androgen insensitivity is a 46,XY disorder of sex development with testes and undervirilized, female-appearing genitalia.
5-alpha-reductase deficiency is a 46,XY disorder of sex development, with testes and undervirilized genitalia from low DHT.
Mixed gonadal dysgenesis is a sex chromosome disorder of sex development, usually with a testis on one side and a streak gonad on the other.
Correct.

topics: Causes of virilization in a female fetus

questions.stem: Because of this infant's enzyme block, 17-hydroxylated 21-carbon precursors accumulate and are converted to 19-carbon androgens such as DHEA and androstenedione. Which of the following enzyme activities carries out this conversion?
approach: 21-hydroxylase deficiency blocks production of cortisol and aldosterone, so precursors such as 17-hydroxyprogesterone build up.
Low cortisol raises ACTH, which pushes even more precursor into the pathway.
To become sex steroids, these 21-carbon precursors must lose their side chain, which is the 17,20-lyase step that forms androstenedione and DHEA.
questions.why: Sex steroid synthesis begins with cholesterol side-chain cleavage to pregnenolone. 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts pregnenolone to progesterone. 17-alpha-hydroxylase adds a hydroxyl group at carbon 17, and 17,20-lyase then cuts off the side chain to make 19-carbon androgens such as androstenedione. 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts androstenedione to testosterone, and aromatase converts androgens to estrogens. In 21-hydroxylase deficiency the 17,20-lyase step carries the trapped precursors into androgens that virilize a female fetus.
whyNot: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens. It acts after androstenedione is formed and would lower androgen, not raise it.
Correct.
17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase acts later, converting androstenedione to testosterone. It does not remove the side chain from 21-carbon precursors.
11-beta-hydroxylase acts after 21-hydroxylase in the cortisol and aldosterone pathways. Its substrates are not formed when 21-hydroxylase is blocked.

questions.stem: A different infant is found to have a 46,XX karyotype in which the SRY gene has been translocated onto one X chromosome. Which of the following gonads is most likely present in that infant?
approach: Recall that SRY is the switch that makes the bipotential gonad become a testis.
It acts by turning on SOX9 in the supporting cells, which then become Sertoli cells.
If SRY is present, testes form, whatever the rest of the karyotype.
questions.why: The early gonad can become either an ovary or a testis. SRY on the Y chromosome turns on SOX9 in supporting cells, which become Sertoli cells and organize testis cords. Once testes form, Sertoli cells make anti-Mullerian hormone and Leydig cells make testosterone, and male development follows. A 46,XX individual with SRY on an X chromosome develops testes and a male phenotype but is infertile, because other Y genes needed for spermatogenesis are missing. In this case's infant, with no SRY, the gonads became ovaries.
whyNot: Correct.
Ovaries form when SRY is absent, as in this case's 46,XX infant without an SRY translocation.
Streak gonads form when germ cells are lost, as in Turner syndrome, or in 46,XY individuals with an SRY deletion or mutation.
An ovary with an ovotestis describes ovotesticular disorder of sex development, which is usually 46,XX without detectable SRY.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman develops a deepening voice, temporal balding, and clitoral enlargement over 4 months. Imaging is pending. Reference ranges are testosterone 15 to 70 ng/dL and DHEA-S 35 to 430 µg/dL. Which of the following serum results most strongly localizes her androgen excess to the adrenal gland?
approach: Separate hirsutism (excess hair only) from virilization (voice change, balding, clitoral enlargement, muscle gain). Rapid virilization suggests an androgen-secreting tumor.
Use the markers: DHEA-S is made almost entirely by the adrenal, while testosterone comes from both the ovary and adrenal.
A very high DHEA-S points to the adrenal. A very high testosterone with normal DHEA-S points to the ovary.
questions.why: Hirsutism is male-pattern hair growth in a woman and is often caused by polycystic ovary syndrome. Virilization means more androgen effect: a deeper voice, temporal balding, clitoral enlargement, and more muscle mass. Rapid virilization suggests a tumor. DHEA-S is a sulfated androgen made almost only by the adrenal cortex, so a markedly raised level localizes the source to the adrenal, as in an adrenal carcinoma or congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A testosterone well above the female range with normal DHEA-S points to the ovary, as in a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor.
whyNot: Both values are normal. This fits idiopathic hirsutism and would not explain rapid virilization.
A mildly raised testosterone with normal DHEA-S is typical of polycystic ovary syndrome, which causes hirsutism but rarely virilization.
Correct.
A markedly raised testosterone with normal DHEA-S localizes the source to the ovary, such as a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor.

dx: Testicular seminoma in a man with a history of cryptorchidism
case: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a painless, heavy feeling in his right testis for 3 months. He had orchiopexy for an undescended right testis at age 3 years. Pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, nontender, enlarged right testis that does not transilluminate. Ultrasonography shows a solid, uniform hypoechoic mass within the testis. Serum studies show an AFP concentration of 4 ng/mL (normal less than 10), beta-hCG concentration of 14 mIU/mL (normal less than 5), and LDH concentration of 420 U/L (normal 100 to 250). He undergoes radical inguinal orchiectomy. Microscopy shows sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei, separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes. The tumor cells stain for placental alkaline phosphatase. Diagnosis: classic seminoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following serum findings, if present, would indicate a nonseminomatous component in this tumor?
approach: Recall which germ cell tumors make which markers: yolk sac tumor makes AFP, choriocarcinoma makes high hCG, and seminoma makes neither AFP nor much hCG.
A mildly raised hCG can occur in pure seminoma from scattered syncytiotrophoblastic cells.
Any raised AFP means a nonseminomatous element, usually yolk sac tumor or embryonal carcinoma.
questions.why: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor. It has sheets of uniform clear cells with lymphocytes in fibrous septa and stains for placental alkaline phosphatase. It is very sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy and has a good prognosis. Pure seminoma does not make AFP. A raised AFP means the tumor contains a nonseminomatous part, such as yolk sac tumor, which changes staging and treatment. Choriocarcinoma makes very high hCG, embryonal carcinoma may raise AFP or hCG, and teratoma usually raises neither.
whyNot: LDH reflects tumor bulk and is raised in many germ cell tumors, including seminoma, so it does not separate types.
A small rise in hCG occurs in some pure seminomas because of scattered syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells. Very high hCG would suggest choriocarcinoma.
Correct.
Placental alkaline phosphatase is a tissue stain that is positive in seminoma. It supports the diagnosis rather than pointing to another type.

topics: Seminoma versus nonseminomatous germ cell tumors

questions.stem: Cytogenetic analysis of this tumor is most likely to show which of the following abnormalities?
approach: Classify the tumor: seminoma is a germ cell tumor, the group that makes up most testicular tumors.
Recall the shared genetic marker of germ cell tumors: extra copies of the short arm of chromosome 12, most often as an isochromosome 12p.
questions.why: About 95% of testicular tumors are germ cell tumors. Most arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ, abnormal germ cells within the seminiferous tubules. Nearly all of these tumors have extra copies of 12p, most often as an isochromosome in which both arms are 12p. Risk factors include cryptorchidism, even after orchiopexy, and Klinefelter syndrome. Sex cord-stromal tumors, such as Leydig cell tumors, are the other main group and do not share this marker.
whyNot: t(11;22) joins EWSR1 and FLI1 and is the marker of Ewing sarcoma of bone and soft tissue.
t(14;18) places BCL2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene and is the marker of follicular lymphoma.
MYCN amplification is a marker of aggressive neuroblastoma.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before his orchiopexy, the undescended testis was at risk for impaired spermatogenesis. Which of the following best explains this risk?
options: Autoimmune injury after breakdown of the blood-testis barrier
Exposure of germ cells to core body temperature
Ischemia from compression of the testicular artery
Lack of LH stimulation of the Leydig cells
approach: Recall that spermatogenesis needs a temperature a few degrees below core body temperature, which the scrotum provides.
An undescended testis sits in the inguinal canal or abdomen at core temperature.
Germ cells are injured by heat, while Leydig cells are relatively spared.
questions.why: The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the body core through the pampiniform plexus countercurrent exchange, the dartos and cremaster muscles, and its thin skin. An undescended testis, most often in the inguinal canal, stays at core temperature, and its germ cells are damaged over time. Sertoli cell function also declines, so inhibin B falls and FSH rises. The cryptorchid testis also carries a higher risk of germ cell tumor, which persists after orchiopexy. Cryptorchidism is more common in preterm infants.
whyNot: Breakdown of the blood-testis barrier can expose sperm antigens after trauma or vasectomy, but it is not the main problem in an undescended testis.
Correct.
Compression of the testicular artery is not the usual mechanism. Acute loss of blood flow happens with torsion, which causes sudden pain.
LH stimulation is not the problem. Leydig cells are relatively spared by heat, so testosterone is usually normal in unilateral cryptorchidism.

questions.stem: The patient's 2-month-old son has a right scrotal swelling that transilluminates. His parents report that it is small on waking and larger by evening. Which of the following best explains the swelling?
approach: A swelling that transilluminates is filled with clear fluid, so it is a hydrocele.
A change in size through the day means the fluid moves between the peritoneal cavity and the scrotum.
That connection is a processus vaginalis that never closed, which is a communicating hydrocele.
questions.why: During descent, the gubernaculum guides the testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, and a pouch of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, goes ahead of it. Normally the processus closes, leaving only the tunica vaginalis around the testis. If it stays open with a narrow channel, peritoneal fluid flows in and out, which is a communicating hydrocele that changes size with activity and position. If the channel is wide enough for bowel, the result is an indirect inguinal hernia.
whyNot: Correct.
A dilated pampiniform plexus is a varicocele. It feels like a bag of worms, usually on the left, and does not transilluminate.
Torsion of the appendix testis causes sudden pain and a small tender nodule at the upper pole, sometimes with a blue dot sign.
The gubernaculum guides descent and becomes the scrotal ligament. It does not hold fluid.

case: A male newborn is examined in the nursery 1 day after an uncomplicated delivery at 38 weeks' gestation. Birth weight is 3100 g. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 44/min. Physical examination shows the urethral opening on the ventral surface of the penis at the junction of the glans and shaft. The foreskin is incomplete ventrally and forms a dorsal hood, and the penis curves ventrally. The scrotum is fused and normally formed. The left testis is in the scrotum, and the right testis is palpable in the inguinal canal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Diagnosis: distal hypospadias with right cryptorchidism.

questions.stem: A different male newborn has a urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis. Which of the following associated anomalies should be sought in that infant?
approach: A dorsal urethral opening is epispadias, a different defect from hypospadias.
Epispadias comes from abnormal position of the genital tubercle, which is also part of the lower abdominal wall defect seen in bladder exstrophy.
Hypospadias, by contrast, goes with cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia.
questions.why: Hypospadias is a ventral urethral opening caused by incomplete fusion of the urethral folds. It is common and is associated with undescended testes and inguinal hernia, as in this infant. Epispadias is a dorsal opening caused by abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle relative to the cloacal membrane. It is rare and is strongly associated with exstrophy of the bladder, in which the bladder is open on the lower abdominal wall.
whyNot: Correct.
Undescended testis is associated with hypospadias, as this infant shows, not specifically with epispadias.
Horseshoe kidney is fusion of the lower poles of the kidneys, seen with Turner syndrome and trisomy 18. It is not linked to a dorsal meatus.
Posterior urethral valves are folds in the prostatic urethra that obstruct urine flow in boys. They are not linked to a dorsal meatus.

questions.stem: The embryonic structures whose incomplete fusion caused this infant's defect develop into which of the following in a female?
approach: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urethral (urogenital) folds on the underside of the developing penis.
In males these folds close to form the penile urethra and the ventral shaft.
In females they stay separate and become the labia minora.
questions.why: The external genitalia start the same in both sexes. The genital tubercle becomes the glans penis or the clitoris. The urethral (urogenital) folds fuse in males to enclose the penile urethra and form the ventral shaft, and stay open in females as the labia minora. The labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum or stay apart as the labia majora. Fusion of the urethral folds depends on DHT, and when it stops early the urethra opens on the ventral surface.
whyNot: The clitoris comes from the genital tubercle, which forms the glans penis in males.
Correct.
The labia majora come from the labioscrotal swellings, which form the scrotum in males. This infant's scrotum is normal.
The lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus, not from the external genital folds.

questions.stem: Another infant, who is 46,XY, has perineal hypospadias, a bifid scrotum, and testes in the labioscrotal folds. Serum testosterone concentration is normal for age, and the ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone is increased. If untreated, which of the following is most likely to occur in that child at puberty?
options: Regression of the testes to streak gonads
Onset of menses from a hypoplastic uterus
approach: A normal testosterone with a high testosterone to DHT ratio means 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency.
Before birth, DHT is needed to form male external genitalia, so they are undervirilized.
At puberty, testosterone rises sharply and can act on the androgen receptor directly, and some DHT forms through the type 1 enzyme, so the body virilizes.
questions.why: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to DHT in genital skin and the prostate. DHT binds the androgen receptor more strongly than testosterone, and it is needed to form the penis, scrotum, and prostate before birth. Without it, the infant has ambiguous or female-appearing genitalia, but normal Wolffian structures and testes. At puberty the large rise in testosterone, plus some DHT from the type 1 enzyme, causes marked virilization, with phallic growth, deepening voice, and muscle gain. Beard growth and male-pattern balding stay limited because they depend on DHT.
whyNot: Breast development without body hair describes complete androgen insensitivity, where androgens cannot act at all.
The testes in this condition are structurally normal and do not regress. Streak gonads occur with gonadal dysgenesis.
Anti-Mullerian hormone from the testes caused the uterus to regress before birth, so there is no uterus to menstruate.
Correct.

questions.stem: Twenty years later, the patient hears a snapping sound during sexual intercourse, followed by immediate loss of erection and rapidly expanding swelling and bruising of the penile shaft. He voids normally with no blood at the meatus. Which of the following structures is most likely torn?
options: Deep dorsal vein of the penis
Tunica albuginea of a corpus cavernosum
Corpus spongiosum and the enclosed urethra
approach: Recognize penile fracture: a snap, sudden detumescence, and a swollen, bruised shaft after forceful bending of the erect penis.
During erection the tunica albuginea around each corpus cavernosum is stretched thin and tense, so it can tear.
Normal voiding with no blood at the meatus makes injury to the corpus spongiosum and urethra less likely.
questions.why: The penis contains three erectile bodies. The paired corpora cavernosa lie dorsally and fill with blood during erection, and the corpus spongiosum lies ventrally around the urethra and expands to form the glans. A tough fibrous sheath, the tunica albuginea, surrounds the corpora cavernosa. In erection it becomes thin and rigid, so sudden bending can tear it. Blood escapes from the corpus, causing the swelling and bruising. A tear that extends into the corpus spongiosum can injure the urethra, which shows up as blood at the meatus or trouble voiding.
whyNot: A torn deep dorsal vein can cause bruising, but it does not produce the snap and sudden loss of erection of a corporal tear.
The suspensory ligament holds the penis to the pubic symphysis. Its injury does not cause sudden loss of erection with shaft hematoma.
Correct.
Injury to the corpus spongiosum often involves the urethra, with blood at the meatus or difficulty voiding, which this patient does not have.

dx: Tubal ectopic pregnancy in an Rh-negative woman with prior salpingitis
case: A 28-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of left lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting for 1 day. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. Three years ago she was treated for salpingitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows left adnexal tenderness. Hemoglobin concentration is 11.0 g/dL (normal 12 to 16). Serum beta-hCG concentration is 2400 mIU/mL, a level at which an intrauterine gestational sac is usually visible. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows no intrauterine gestational sac, a left adnexal mass, and a small amount of free pelvic fluid. Her blood type is O, Rh(D)-negative; her partner is Rh(D)-positive. Diagnosis: left ampullary tubal ectopic pregnancy.

questions.stem: In a later pregnancy, the blastocyst implants in the lower uterine segment, and the placenta develops over the internal cervical os. Which of the following is the most likely complication of this placental position?
options: Painful vaginal bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus
Uterine rupture early in the course of labor
Painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester
approach: Identify the condition: a placenta covering the internal os is placenta previa, a form of abnormal implantation site, as is tubal ectopic pregnancy.
As the lower uterine segment stretches and the cervix begins to change late in pregnancy, the placenta separates from its attachment.
Separation exposes maternal vessels, causing painless, bright red bleeding.
questions.why: Normal implantation occurs in the upper posterior wall of the uterine body. Implantation outside the uterus, most often in the ampulla of the uterine tube, is an ectopic pregnancy, and prior salpingitis is a major risk factor. Implantation low in the uterus can place the placenta over the internal os, which is placenta previa. In the third trimester the lower segment thins and stretches, the placenta shears off, and painless vaginal bleeding results. Placenta previa also raises the risk of placenta accreta, especially after a prior cesarean delivery.
whyNot: Painful bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus describes placental abruption, a premature separation of a normally placed placenta.
Severe hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks is preeclampsia, which relates to abnormal spiral artery remodeling, not placental position.
Uterine rupture is linked mainly to a prior uterine scar, such as a previous cesarean delivery, not to placenta previa alone.
Correct.

questions.stem: At laparoscopy, thin fibrous adhesions are seen stretching between the anterior surface of the liver and the diaphragm. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Perihepatitis from spread of the earlier tubal infection
Hematogenous seeding of the liver forming an abscess
Adhesions from leakage of blood from the ectopic pregnancy
approach: Recognize the violin-string adhesions between liver capsule and diaphragm as Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.
Link it to her earlier chlamydial salpingitis: organisms spread from the open end of the tube along the right paracolic gutter to the liver capsule.
The same past infection scarred the tube, which is why the embryo implanted there.
questions.why: Salpingitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae can damage the tube and the peritoneum. Scarring of the tubal lining and loss of cilia slow transport of the embryo, which raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility. Infection can also form a hydrosalpinx or a tubo-ovarian abscess. When organisms spread up the right paracolic gutter, they inflame the liver capsule, causing right upper quadrant pain at the time and later leaving violin-string adhesions. This is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.
whyNot: Correct.
Ascending cholangitis is infection inside the bile ducts, with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. It does not form capsular adhesions to the diaphragm.
A pyogenic liver abscess is a collection inside the liver tissue, not thin adhesions on the surface.
Blood from a tubal pregnancy collects in the pelvis. It does not produce organized adhesions on the liver surface.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the process that could harm a later Rh(D)-positive fetus if this patient becomes sensitized by fetal red cells during this ectopic pregnancy?
options: Maternal anti-D IgM crossing the placenta to activate complement
Fetal anti-D IgG damaging maternal red cells in the placenta
Maternal anti-D IgG crossing the placenta to coat fetal red cells
Maternal cytotoxic T cells entering the fetus to lyse fetal red cells
approach: Fetal red cells that enter the circulation of an Rh-negative mother trigger an antibody response against the D antigen.
The first response is IgM, but memory B cells switch to IgG, and IgG crosses the placenta by FcRn transport.
In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, IgG coats fetal red cells, and fetal macrophages destroy them. This is type II hypersensitivity.
questions.why: Fetal blood can enter the maternal circulation during delivery, miscarriage, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, or trauma. An Rh(D)-negative mother exposed to Rh(D)-positive fetal cells can form anti-D antibodies. The first pregnancy is usually spared because the early response is mainly IgM and is slow. In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, memory cells quickly make anti-D IgG, which crosses the placenta, binds fetal red cells, and leads to their destruction in the fetal spleen. Severe hemolysis causes anemia, heart failure, and hydrops fetalis. Anti-D immune globulin given after the ectopic pregnancy prevents sensitization.
whyNot: IgM is a large pentamer and does not cross the placenta, so it cannot reach the fetus.
The fetus does not make antibodies against its mother's red cells. The harmful antibody comes from the mother.
Correct.
Hemolytic disease of the fetus is antibody-mediated (type II). Maternal T cells do not cause it.

questions.stem: Fertilization of the oocyte took place in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Immediately after the first sperm fused with the oocyte membrane, which of the following events prevented additional sperm from entering?
options: Acrosomal release of enzymes from the sperm head
Exocytosis of cortical granules that alters the zona
Completion of meiosis I with release of a polar body
Capacitation of sperm within the uterine tube
approach: Recall that the block to polyspermy comes from the oocyte, not the sperm.
Sperm fusion triggers a rise in calcium inside the oocyte.
Calcium releases cortical granules, whose enzymes change the zona pellucida so other sperm cannot bind or pass through.
questions.why: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the widest part of the uterine tube. Capacitated sperm undergo the acrosome reaction, release enzymes, and penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida. When the first sperm fuses with the oocyte, a wave of calcium causes cortical granules to release their contents. Their enzymes modify the zona pellucida so it no longer binds sperm, which is the cortical (zona) reaction. The oocyte then completes meiosis II, releases the second polar body, and forms the female pronucleus.
whyNot: The acrosome reaction lets a sperm penetrate the zona pellucida. It helps fertilization rather than blocking extra sperm.
Correct.
Meiosis I is completed before ovulation. At fertilization the oocyte completes meiosis II.
Capacitation happens before fertilization and prepares sperm to bind the zona. It does not block polyspermy.

dx: Septate uterus with recurrent pregnancy loss
case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of three consecutive pregnancy losses at 9 to 11 weeks' gestation. Her menstrual cycles are regular every 28 days. Pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a single cervix and a normal vagina. Three-dimensional ultrasonography shows a uterus with a smooth, convex outer fundal contour and a midline septum dividing the upper uterine cavity into two parts. Both kidneys are normal. Karyotypes of both partners are normal, antiphospholipid antibody tests are negative, and serum TSH concentration is 2.1 µU/mL (normal 0.5 to 5.0). Diagnosis: septate uterus with recurrent pregnancy loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following developmental errors best explains this patient's ultrasonographic findings?
options: Complete failure of the paramesonephric ducts to fuse
Failure to resorb the midline wall after duct fusion
Incomplete fusion of the paramesonephric ducts at the fundus
Failure of one paramesonephric duct to develop
approach: The uterus forms when the paramesonephric ducts fuse in the midline, and the wall between them is then resorbed.
A normal outer fundal contour means fusion was complete. A midline septum inside means the wall between the ducts did not resorb.
Bicornuate and didelphys uteri show a notched or doubled outer contour because fusion itself failed.
questions.why: The two paramesonephric ducts first fuse side by side, which shapes the outer uterus, and then the septum between them is resorbed to create one cavity. In a septate uterus, fusion is complete, so the outer contour is smooth, but the septum persists. The septum is fibromuscular and poorly vascularized, so an embryo that implants on it is poorly supplied, which leads to pregnancy loss. Abnormal fusion or canalization lower down can leave a longitudinal or transverse vaginal septum.
whyNot: Complete failure of fusion produces uterus didelphys, with two separate uterine bodies and two cervices. This patient has one cervix.
Correct.
Partial failure of fusion at the top produces a bicornuate uterus, with a heart-shaped outer contour and a notch in the fundus.
Failure of one duct produces a unicornuate uterus, often with a kidney anomaly on the side of the missing duct. Her kidneys are normal.

questions.stem: During a later pregnancy, removal of the corpus luteum at 6 weeks' gestation would likely cause pregnancy loss, but removal at 14 weeks would not. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: The fetal adrenal gland begins to secrete progesterone
Maternal pituitary LH output rises after 12 weeks
The placenta becomes the main source of progesterone
hCG concentration peaks and directly supports the decidua
approach: Early pregnancy needs progesterone to keep the decidua intact, and at first the corpus luteum supplies it.
hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast acts on LH receptors to keep the corpus luteum alive.
Near the end of the first trimester, the placenta makes enough progesterone by itself, so the corpus luteum is no longer needed.
questions.why: After implantation, the syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, which acts like LH and keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone. Progesterone maintains the decidua and keeps the myometrium quiet. The placenta also makes progesterone from maternal cholesterol, and between about 7 and 10 weeks its output becomes large enough to replace the corpus luteum. By the end of the first trimester the corpus luteum is no longer needed. This is the luteal-placental shift. Placental estriol is different, because the placenta lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase and needs DHEA-S from the fetal adrenal to make it.
whyNot: The fetal adrenal supplies DHEA-S, which the placenta uses to make estriol. It is not a main source of progesterone.
Maternal LH is suppressed during pregnancy by high estrogen and progesterone, so it does not rise.
Correct.
hCG peaks at about 8 to 10 weeks and then falls. It supports the corpus luteum, not the decidua directly.

questions.stem: In each of her pregnancies, the conceptus began to implant about 6 days after fertilization. Which of the following layers of the conceptus invades the endometrium and secretes the hormone detected by a pregnancy test?
approach: Trace the conceptus: zygote, morula, then blastocyst, with an inner cell mass and an outer trophoblast.
At implantation the trophoblast splits into an inner cytotrophoblast and an outer syncytiotrophoblast.
The syncytiotrophoblast erodes the endometrium and secretes hCG, the hormone measured in a pregnancy test.
questions.why: The zygote divides as it moves down the uterine tube, becomes a morula, and then a blastocyst that enters the uterus. At about day 6 the blastocyst attaches to the endometrium. Its outer trophoblast forms the cytotrophoblast, a layer of dividing cells, and the syncytiotrophoblast, a multinucleated layer without cell borders. The syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium and makes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum active. The inner cell mass forms the epiblast and hypoblast, which build the embryo and yolk sac.
whyNot: Correct.
The cytotrophoblast is the inner, dividing layer that supplies cells to the syncytiotrophoblast. It does not itself invade or secrete most hCG.
Extraembryonic mesoderm forms in the second week between the trophoblast and the yolk sac and lines the chorionic cavity. It does not invade the endometrium.
The hypoblast is part of the inner cell mass and helps form the yolk sac.

questions.stem: Before her next attempt at conception, she is advised to begin daily folic acid supplementation to lower the risk of a neural tube defect. A deficiency of folate most directly impairs which of the following reactions?
options: Hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen
Methylation of dUMP to form dTMP
approach: Folate carries one-carbon units as tetrahydrofolate derivatives.
Thymidylate synthase uses methylene-tetrahydrofolate to methylate dUMP to dTMP, which is needed to make DNA. Folate also supplies carbons for purine synthesis.
Rapidly dividing neural tube cells need a large supply of DNA precursors, and the tube must close by about day 28.
questions.why: Folate in the form of tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon groups for DNA synthesis. Thymidylate synthase uses N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate to convert dUMP to dTMP, and folate also donates two carbons to the purine ring. Low folate slows DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. The neural tube closes by about day 28 after fertilization, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so supplementation must begin before conception.
whyNot: Homocysteine conversion to cystathionine is catalyzed by cystathionine beta-synthase and needs vitamin B6, not folate.
Methylmalonyl-CoA conversion to succinyl-CoA needs vitamin B12. It is not affected by folate deficiency.
Hydroxylation of proline in collagen needs vitamin C. Its deficiency causes scurvy.
Correct.
